# The Tale of the First Shadow

Long ago, when the world was newly born, the Sun blazed alone in an empty sky, casting light upon everything without rest. There were no shadows, for the Sun's brilliance touched all corners of the earth simultaneously.

A young weaver named Sola grew tired of the endless light. Her eyes ached, and she longed for rest, but sleep would not come in the perpetual brightness. In desperation, she climbed the highest mountain and called out to the Sun.

"Great Sun," she pleaded, "your gift of light is precious, but without darkness, we cannot appreciate your beauty. Grant us respite."

The Sun, who had never considered this, felt compassion. But it could not dim itself without plunging the world into cold darkness. So it made a bargain with Sola.

"Weave me a cloak," said the Sun, "and I will wear it as I travel, creating patches of rest beneath."

Sola wove for seven days, creating the first darkness from threads of night-blooming flowers. When finished, the Sun draped the cloak across the land as it moved, and thus shadows were born—gifts of rest following the Sun's journey, teaching humanity that even light needs darkness to be truly appreciated.

From that crack, water began to flow—the mountain's tears of yearning, transformed into something new. The water carved a path down his slopes, singing as it traveled, seeing all the wonders the mountain could not reach.

The mountain realized he had created the first river—a part of himself that could journey everywhere he dreamed of going. Through the river's song, he experienced distant oceans, forests, and plains.

This is why rivers always sing: they carry the ancient voice of mountains, telling stories of everything they witness on their endless journey to the sea, fulfilling the wanderlust of stone.

"I am the bridge," she realized, "between brightness and darkness."
